abstracts.abstract: This paper establishes a fundamental connection between combinatorial designs and code-based cryptography, introducing a novel paradigm that leverages design-theoretic structures to address security challenges in post-quantum cryptographic systems. Traditional code-based schemes rely on the hardness of decoding random linear codes, yet their security proofs often lack geometric insight into code structure. We demonstrate that symmetric designs, particularly finite projective planes and their derived structures, give rise to a new class of codes with remarkable cryptographic properties. By analyzing the covering radius and distinguishing the computational complexity of decoding structured codes derived from resolvable 2-designs, we prove that these constructions offer resistance to known attack strategies. Our theoretical framework reveals that the inherent symmetry of design structures creates natural correlations that can be exploited for improved security guarantees while maintaining practical key sizes. The analysis extends to examining the relationship between design parameters and fundamental cryptographic hardness assumptions, providing a unified perspective that connects previously disparate areas of design theory and cryptographic coding. This work opens new avenues for constructing cryptographic primitives with provable security foundations grounded in combinatorial structure theory.

This paper presents a significant improvement to the theoretical understanding of quasi-cyclic codes over finite fields by establishing new connections between algebraic structure and minimum distance bounds. While quasi-cyclic codes have been extensively studied for their favorable encoding and decoding complexity, previous bounds on their minimum distance have been insufficient for optimal code construction. We develop a novel approach using the representation theory of cyclic groups combined with algebraic methods over finite fields to derive sharper Singleton-type bounds for this important class of codes. Our analysis demonstrates that the concatenated structure of quasi-cyclic codes admits much better distance profiles than previously known, particularly for codes over fields of characteristic two. We establish that for any given length and dimension, there exist quasi-cyclic codes whose minimum distance exceeds the classical bound by a factor that grows with the co-index, providing constructive evidence for these theoretical improvements. The techniques introduced extend naturally to multi-twisted codes and reveal fundamental limitations in previous asymptotic analyses. These results have immediate implications for the construction of efficient algebraic coding schemes in both storage and communication applications.

This paper introduces a fundamentally novel approach to secure network coding that utilizes combinatorial design theory to construct information-theoretically secure transmission schemes for multicast networks. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on computational assumptions or pre-shared keys, our design-based framework achieves unconditional security against eavesdropping attacks with arbitrarily many colluding adversaries. The proposed protocol leverages the structural properties of t-designs to create naturally private encoding operations, where the algebraic structure itself prevents adversaries from gaining meaningful information about transmitted messages. We develop explicit constructions for practical network scenarios, demonstrating that design-theoretic network codes achieve security guarantees that are impossible to attain with traditional random linear network coding. The system architecture supports dynamic network topologies and provides efficient encoding and decoding algorithms with polynomial-time complexity. Security analysis formally proves that any coalition of up to t internal nodes learns no additional information beyond what is necessarily revealed by the network topology. This work establishes a new paradigm where combinatorial structure serves as the source of cryptographic security rather than computational hardness, with immediate applications in secure broadcasting, distributed storage, and quantum key distribution networks.

This paper presents an improved construction methodology for quantum stabilizer codes that substantially advances the state-of-the-art in quantum error correction. While existing approaches to quantum code construction have relied primarily on CSS construction from classical codes or operator algebra techniques, we introduce a systematic framework that exploits the rich structure of combinatorial designs to construct quantum codes with superior parameters. Our method transforms well-understood classical codes with specific divisibility properties into quantum codes with improved encoding rates and distance thresholds. The practical implementation includes efficient encoding circuits with reduced depth compared to previous constructions, making these codes more viable for near-term quantum computing architectures. We provide explicit constructions achieving parameters that exceed known bounds for the relevant code length ranges, demonstrating concrete improvements for quantum memories and fault-tolerant computation. The decoding algorithm maintains manageable complexity while achieving error correction performance that surpasses existing techniques. Complexity analysis and simulation results confirm the practical viability of the proposed scheme, with improved threshold estimates under realistic noise models. This work provides both theoretical justification and practical tools for leveraging combinatorial structures in quantum information processing applications.
